Wells of Salvation
WELZ uv sal-VAY-shun
n. pl. (the inexhaustible springs from which the redeemed draw)
Hebrew mayenei ha-yeshuah, the springs of salvation, from mayan, a spring or fountain, from ayin, an eye — a spring being the eye of the earth — with yeshuah, salvation. The phrase occurs once in the Authorized Version.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

The wells of salvation appear once, at the end of Isaiah's song of the redeemed: “Therefore with joy shall ye draw water out of the wells of salvation” (Isaiah 12:3). The Hebrew is mayan, not a cistern but a living spring, and the word is built on ayin, an eye, because a spring is the eye of the earth where water looks out. Three things are given in the one verse. The water is drawn, which means salvation is appropriated and not merely admired — there is a bucket and an arm in the picture. It is drawn with joy, which makes gladness the proper manner of the Christian life and not an optional temperament. And the source is wells in the plural, springs that do not fail, because what is drawn from them was never the drawer's to begin with. Isaiah 12 is a song appointed for a day of restoration, sung by a people who had been under the cup of trembling and had it taken out of their hand. Our Lord takes the figure up at the feast of tabernacles, at the very moment the water was being drawn and poured in the temple, and stands and cries that the thirsty should come to Him and drink, and that out of the believer's belly shall flow rivers of living water.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): Wells of salvation, the living springs of God's saving mercy, from which the redeemed draw with joy; Hebrew mayan, a spring, from ayin, an eye.

Hebrew mayan, a spring, a fountain, a living well.

From ayin, an eye; a spring is the eye of the earth.

Hebrew yeshuah, salvation, deliverance, from yasha, to save.

The phrase occurs once, Isaiah 12:3.

Taken up by Christ at the feast of tabernacles, John 7:37-38.

Key Scripture

Isa 12:3 — "Therefore with joy shall ye draw water out of the wells of salvation."

Isa 12:2 — "Behold, God is my salvation; I will trust, and not be afraid: for the LORD JEHOVAH is my strength and my song; he also is become my salvation."

Joh 7:37 — "In the last day, that great day of the feast, Jesus stood and cried, saying, If any man thirst, let him come unto me, and drink."

Joh 4:14 — "But whosoever drinketh of the water that I shall give him shall never thirst; but the water that I shall give him shall be in him a well of water springing up into everlasting life."

Modern Corruption

Salvation is treated as a transaction completed and shelved, rather than a spring to be drawn from daily and with gladness.

expand to see more

Two errors are answered by the one verse. The first treats salvation as a single past transaction, filed and finished, so that the believer has nothing left to do with it but remember the date. Isaiah puts a bucket in his hand and tells him to draw. The second is the opposite error of the sacramental systems, which make the well a cistern under the church's management, so that grace is dispensed by an institution rather than drawn by the thirsty. Mayan is a spring, not a reservoir, and springs are not administered.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the duty and the gladness of appropriation. The means of grace — the word read and preached, prayer, the ordinances, the assembly of the saints — are the buckets, and a Christian who owns a well and never lowers anything into it will be thirsty in the middle of plenty. Isaiah says the drawing is done with joy, which is the note most commonly missing. A dutiful, joyless drawing has misread the verse by half.
